correctness.rationale: The exact translated trace is μ and determinant is ω²−cμ; dI/dμ=−ω²/(2cs) at the crossing. The scalar elimination reconstructs the recovery variable without time change. For rigorous amplitude expansions write x=r(cos τ+y) with y orthogonal to both first harmonics, divide the periodic equation by signed r, and use the implicit-function theorem near (y,μ,Ω)=(0,0,ω). The y derivative ω²(∂τ²+1) is invertible on the complementary modes; the μ and Ω derivatives span the two first harmonics because their sine and cosine pivots are ω and −2ω. The quadratic forcing has no first harmonic, so μ and Ω have no linear terms. Inverting on the other modes gives the stated X₂. Direct projection at the next order gives sine coefficient ω/4−cs²/(2ω)−mω and cosine coefficient s²/3+5c²s²/(6ω²)−c/4+cm. Vanishing sine fixes m; the remaining cosine is s²(1+c²/ω²)/3 and balances −2ων. This gives K=−ν/ω>0. The nonzero m and unit trace crossing give the unique local Hopf family on μ/m>0. Independently, the mean cycle divergence μ−2U⟨x⟩−⟨x²⟩ equals −mr²+O(r³), so the transverse multiplier gives the stated stability. For μ<0 small the linear squared frequency exceeds ω² by |μ|(c−|μ|/4)>0, yielding the opposite linear-period change.
residual_risks: The symbolic and numeric support is corroboration. In the shooting code the displayed trial amplitude is set through the leading μ–amplitude law, not measured as an exact Fourier amplitude.

value.rationale: Physical-time period drift is an observable quantity independent of how the Hopf criticality is classified. A uniform sign across both stability types is a model-specific result, and the subcritical branch makes a linear frequency estimate predict the opposite direction from the actual periodic orbit. The coefficient applies to a concrete measured harmonic rather than an arbitrary state-space radius.
